title: The Surviving Fragments of the Poem
html:
Fifteen fragments of the poem printed in the 1971 edition (Bibliotheca Indica series) on pp. 10–222; the Bengali text was transcribed by the Exeter "Famine and Dearth" project.

Fragment 1. Nadia-khanda, section 1 (1971 ed., p. 10)

The village of Jayapura in Srihatta; its brahmanas; the lineage of Jagannatha Mishra and his marriage to Shachi; a prophecy that Nanda and Yashoda, Dasharatha and Kaushalya will be born in brahmana families

[Then the narrative; disha.]1

1In the land of Srihatta there is a village, Jayapura,
a place full of every delight, without equal on earth.

2There are long ponds, lakes, wells, tanks with flights of steps,
temples and shrines, monasteries, many flower gardens.

3Houses of carpenters' work,2 town squares,
brick-built gateways within the enclosing walls.

4Dance-halls, schools, four-walled pavilions, cottages with curved roofs,
flags; kalahamsa geese and doves at play.3

5Coconut palms, jackfruit trees, areca palms, mangoes, banyans,
and close by bakula, champaka, tala palms, kadamba.

6Ashvattha, tamarind, nim, jambu, date palms,
oranges, citrons, bilva, the clove tree […].4

7Pillars painted with vermilion and orpiment, with marks of moon and sun;5
peacocks, cranes and parrots perch at the doorways.

8Pavilions, platforms, watch-towers, many halls for the study of the shastras,
palaces, temples, water-sheds, rows of latticed windows.6

9To the east is the Sarasvati, to the north the Gomati,
to the west the Dhol-samudra, to the south the Karati.7

10All the brahmana households in Jayapura
are men of godlike form, great learning and great wealth.

11Born of the great house of Ravi,8 of a great lineage,
conquerors of the quarters, expounding their own darshanas like four-faced Brahma.

12In such a lineage Jagannatha Mishra was born;
Nilambara Chakravarti gave him Shachi in marriage.

13Close by was born Vasudeva Chakravarti.9

14Nanda and Yashoda, taking the water of the Yamuna in hand, vowed:10
"Rama and Krishna shall surely be born in my line."

15Ekachakra, the village of Khalakapura, is a lovely place;
the lovely land of Rarh is like Gokula of old.

16There Nanda and Yashoda will be born in a line of the twice-born,
taking at last the names Padmavati and Paramananda.11

17In a brahmana family Dasharatha and the chaste Kaushalya
took the names Madhavananda and Labhyamati.12

18Who will be born in which lineage in the joy of prema —
all this I shall tell one by one in the Uttara-khanda.

19Meditating on the two feet of Chaitanya and Gadadhara,
Jayananda composes something of the Chaitanya-mangala.

Fragment 2. Nadia-khanda, section 2 (1971 ed., pp. 10–11)

Lawlessness, famine, drought and pestilence in Srihatta; Nilambara Chakravarti and Jagannatha Mishra move with all their kin to the bank of the Ganga, to Navadvipa

[Narrative; disha.]

1In the land of Srihatta lawlessness and famine arose;
dacoity, theft, drought and pestilence set in.

2The land fell into ruin; seeing the calamity,
all the people fled away to various lands.

3Nilambara Chakravarti and Mishra Jagannatha
with all their kin left Jayapura because of the troubles.

4"In what land shall we live?" all of them reasoned.
"In this land we shall find no protection; let us go elsewhere.

5A dwelling fit for us all is on the bank of the Ganga,
just as Nanda left Gokula because of its calamities.

6Long ago a king of ascetics told me:
'Leave this land and go into the very midst of Nadia.'

7A lawless land is not fit to live in;
in Srihatta not half a sesame seed's worth of good people remains.

8One should live among people whose longing, love and mind are for Krishna, where they love the tirthas, love meditation,13 where ascetics live who have conquered the senses,

9where they have faith in the Ganga, the Vaishnavas and mahaprasada —
in people of little fortune these things are not manifest.

10We shall bathe in the Ganga and live in Navadvipa:
that is living in Vaikuntha — what need then of japa and austerity?"

11Riding in fine palanquins, Mishra came with his kin,
and he saw the Ganga and Navadvipa and floated in the bliss of prema.

12Navadvipa is heaven on earth in all the circle of the world;
people of many classes live on the bank of the Jahnavi.

13Meditating on the lotus feet of Chaitanya-chandra,
Jayananda sings the Lord's mangala in bliss.

Fragment 3. Nadia-khanda, section 3 (1971 ed., pp. 11–13)

In praise of the city of Nadia: its temples, markets and people — gods and gandharvas incarnate; vessels, ornaments and fabrics in Mishra's house and in the markets of Nadia

[Raga Suhi.]

1A city wondrous with many paintings and colours,
where people of many castes dwell;
temples and shrines plastered with lime,
trees and creepers of every hue.

2Glory, glory to the blessed city of Nadia
on the bank of the Alakananda!
Kamala, the lovely, plays there,
adorned with bakula garlands.

3On every house a wondrous finial pot,
fluttering banners fly;
as once was the city of Ayodhya —
they flash like strokes of lightning.

4Dance-halls, schools, long ponds, lakes,
wells, tanks with flights of steps;
monasteries, pavilions, well-built courtyards,
gardens of kunda jasmine and tulasi.

5At every door painted panels shine,
in every lane a market is held;
in every lane joyous dancing and song,
in every house the recitation of the Veda.

6Taking the form of the twice-born, gods and gandharvas
were born in Navadvipa;
becoming brahmanas' wives, Indra's vidyadharis
sing beside the Ganga.

7Leaving heaven, all the hosts of gandharvas
were born as vaidyas and their wives;14
gods, rishis and munis, taking the form of brahmanas,
study the shruti and the Gita.

8At the hour of cow-dust, mridangas and fans there,
canopies gleam […];
courtyards walled with brick,
well-made doors of houses.15

9Glass and shields painted with vermilion and orpiment,
four-walled pavilions, four-sided halls;
in the halls handsome, massive pillars
adorned with marks of moon and sun.

10Peacocks, parrots, cranes, doves,
fans shaped as lions and swans;
wondrous yak-tail whisks, canopies,
in every house fine conch-shell bangles.16

11Basins, betel boxes, areca caskets,
mirrors, little cups for unguents;17
copper pots, brass pitchers for juices,
tripods from Varanasi.

12Betel boxes inlaid with conch-shell, sarangi platters,
bowls all full of sweets;
[…] spouted water-pots, copper […],
cool brass ewers.18

13Stone vessels of fine workmanship,
sticks of chalk and paint;19
Oriya and Gaudiya locks and combs,
wondrous little caskets.

14Tar bracelets, strings of cowries, golden amulets,
armlets, wrist-bangles, jewelled anklets;
gold ornaments shaped like ketaki leaves, coral, pearls,
[wares] from the land of Kashmir.20

15Gold leaf, […] betel, […],
wondrous beni braids from the land of Kanchi;
silks, fine muslins, Tibetan cloth, saklat broadcloth, blankets,
shriram-khani and jamakha fabrics;
sapphires from Tibet,
lakshmi-vilasa and taraka cloths.21

16I cannot write how many servants and maids
toil in Mishra's house;
whatever is rare in all the worlds
is sold in the market of Nadia.

17Meditating on the honey of the lotus feet
of Chaitanya and Gadadhara, the lord of his life,
the brahmana Jayananda sings the Chaitanya-mangala,
the deep secret of the nigamas.

Fragment 4. Nadia-khanda, section 4 (1971 ed., pp. 13–15)

The birth and youth of Nityananda; the birth of Advaita; Jagannatha Mishra and the birth of Vishvarupa; famine in Navadvipa; the king of Gauda persecutes the brahmanas on the slander of the yavanas of Piralya; Sarvabhauma's flight to Utkala; the king's dream of Kali and the restoration of Navadvipa

[Narrative; disha.]

1Blessed, blessed among the seven islands is Jambudvipa;
blessed, blessed is the land of Gauda near Utkala.

2In Ekachakra-Khalakapura, from the womb of Padmavati,
Ananta was born in the month of Magha, in the bright fortnight.

3After the birth rite they gave the Thakura a name;
playing childish games, he revealed himself in many ways.

4Seeing his madness, his detachment and great boldness,
they gave him the sacred thread and set him to study in a school of shastra.

5Mother, father and brothers saw many of his manifestations;
in his eighteenth year he left home.

6At Prayaga was the king of ascetics, Ishvara Puri;
there, taking him as guru, he accepted sannyasa,22

7and, an Avadhuta in prema, took the name Nityananda;
having visited all the tirthas, he settled in Kashi.

8In Vanga, in the village of Bamanabala, lived Labhyavati Thakurani;
from her womb was born Advaita, the crest-jewel.23

9While in the lying-in chamber he was called Kamalaksha;
later, in full manifestation, he would bear the title Advaita.

10To Shachi eight daughters were born in due time;
by the bond of fate some time went by.

11Jagannatha Mishra became Mishra Purandara —
a good poet, a pandita, a great logician, handsome.

12Seeing his severe austerity, all people marvelled:
bathing, sandhya, the daily shraddha, worship of the gods,

13offerings, homa, japa, sandhya, puja with incense and lamps,
reading the Srimad Bhagavata before Govinda.

14Another son was born, named Vishvarupa;
a great famine arose in the village of Navadvipa.

15Seeing the calamity — incessant dacoity and theft —
all the people fled away to various lands.

16Then Jagannatha Mishra joyfully
performed Vishvarupa's ten rites one after another.

17Suddenly in Navadvipa there came fear of the king:
seizing brahmanas, the king takes their caste and their life.

18In whatever house in Navadvipa he hears the sound of a conch,
he takes its owner's wealth and life and destroys his caste.

19If he sees tilaka on a forehead, a sacred thread on a shoulder,
he loots house and home and binds the man in iron fetters.

20He breaks temples and shrines, uproots the tulasi;
in fear for their lives the people of Navadvipa have no peace.

21He forbade bathing in the Ganga at all the markets and ghats;
ashvattha and jackfruit trees are cut down by hundreds.

22All the yavanas who lived in the village of Piralya24
brought ruin on the brahmanas of Navadvipa.

23Strife between brahmanas and yavanas has gone on from age to age;
the dreadful village of Piralya lies near Navadvipa.

24Before the lord of Gauda they made a false accusation:
"The brahmanas of Navadvipa will bring you calamity.

25There is a prophecy that a brahmana will become king in Gauda;
do not be careless, lest calamity follow.

26A brahmana of Navadvipa will surely become king;
it is written by the gandharvas that his subjects will bear bows."25

27This lie lodged in the king's mind,
and the king gave the order: "Lay Nadia waste!"

28Visharada's son, Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya,
went with his whole family to Utkala, leaving the kingdom of Gauda.

29In Utkala the warlike king Prataparudra
honoured Sarvabhauma on a jewelled throne.

30His brother Vidya-vachaspati stayed on in Gauda;
Visharada took up residence in Varanasi.

31Vidya-virinchi and Vidyaranya in Navadvipa,
Bhattacharya-shiromani in the sight of all.26

32The lord of Gauda heard that Nadia had been laid waste,
and at night he saw a most terrible dream.

33Kali, bearing sword and skull-cup, naked,
a garland of heads on her neck, crying "Cut! Cut!" —

34seizing the king by the hair, she drove a spear into his chest
and poured boiling oil into his ears and nostrils:

35"Today I will throw your capital of Gauda into the Ganga;
I will cut down your whole line, your elephants, horses and troops!"

36The lord of Gauda says: "Mother, spare my body!
Today I will resettle Navadvipa — save my life!"

37The king rubbed his nose on the ground,27 and then Kali let him go;
the lord of Gauda fainted and fell to the earth.

38In the morning he told the dream to his confidant;
hearing of the wondrous dream, all people were seized with dread.

39"The command of the lord of Gauda: let Navadvipa dwell in happiness;
there is no royal tax — let all people plough their fields.

40Whoever from today obstructs the markets and ghats
shall pay a fine to the treasury and be impaled on the stake.28

41Whoever breaks temples and shrines, whoever cuts an ashvattha —
impale him on a stake in the market of Nadia.

42Let all the vaidyas and brahmanas who live in Navadvipa
hold all manner of festivals to their hearts' content.

43Let dance, song and music sound in every house;
let banners fly on the finials above the temples.

44Let there be flower markets, a profusion of perfumes;
let conch, bell and instruments sound with cries of victory.

45As Navadvipa was a capital in former days,
let it be heard of as a hundred times greater.

46If you see a yavana within the bounds of Navadvipa,
kill him at your own will — or else spare him.29

47Worship the gods in happiness, perform sacrifice, homa and charity;
the markets and ghats are not forbidden — bathe in the Ganga.

48What authority have I over the subjects of Navadvipa?
Truly, truly I say: they are the essence of the world."

49By the king's command Navadvipa was created anew;
in autumn, at the end of the night, there was a rain of flowers.

50The great men who had left the village
all came back, their wishes fulfilled.30

51Meditating on the two feet of Chaitanya and Gadadhara,
Jayananda composes the Nadia-khanda in bliss.

Fragment 5. Nadia-khanda, section 9 (1971 ed., p. 19)

A lullaby: the infant Gauranga cries, and Shachi fears the evil eye and illness; the Lord's crying is a pretence

[Narrative; disha. Raga Barari.]

1"Why do you cry, my little one, bringing up your milk again and again?
You won't stay in my arms, you won't open your eyes.31

2I don't know what pain has come into your little belly;
how little you eat — you will be the death of your mother!32

3O lullaby, lullaby!
Why does my Gauranga Raya cry?33

4Who has looked upon your shapely little body?
I don't know what demon has seized you.34

5You won't take the breast in your mouth, your little body is hot —
from where has an evil wind fallen upon my son?"

6Seeing his mother's grief, Gauranga-chand
fell asleep in her arms and cried no more.

7So Shachi Thakurani's wish was fulfilled;35
Jayananda says: the Lord's crying was a pretence.

Fragment 6. Nadia-khanda, section 11 (1971 ed., pp. 20–21)

Childhood games on the bank of the Ganga; the Ganga circles Gauranga; Shachi's lament; the boy sits on a heap of discarded pots and teaches about Brahman

[Narrative; disha.]

1Another day at dawn, with all the boys,
he played merrily at childish games on the bank of the river of the gods.

2Beds, seats, thrones, dwellings of sand;
someone builds a temple of sand.

3In the sand temple they cook rice and curries;
someone makes an offering to a sand Gopinatha.

4Some say: "Brother, let's eat mahaprasada!"
Another says: "Come, brother, let's play kaya-kheri!"36

5All around, the boys splash in the waters of the Ganga,
and in their midst Gauranga-chand revealed himself.

6The Ganga is overwhelmed with prema, her waters do not flow;
under the guise of waves the Ganga circles round him.

7Meanwhile Shachi Thakurani looked for him from house to house,
and, learning where he was, went to the bank of the river of the gods:

8"You went out to play when the night was over —
seven ghatis have passed;37 why don't you come home?

9My father's deity, child of a mother who lost her children,
O my lord, my life, true fruit of Shachi's womb!38

10O my priceless treasure, O object of my meditation,
O deity of my house, O my life!"

11Hearing his mother's lament, he was moved to pity;
gathering up his game of kaya-kheri, he went home.

12Entering his house by the high road,
he gave a great shout and leapt into the pit of leftovers.

13Gathering all the discarded pots in one place,
he sat on top of them and expounded Brahman:

14"Regard all beings as equal, be compassionate to them as to yourself;
the difference between filth and sandal — all of it is maya.

15So long as this is not manifest in the body,
so long one must not fall away from worldly rules."39

16Having told such realization in detail,
he ran, sucked at the breast, and laughed in Shachi's arms.

17Meditating on the two feet of Chaitanya and Gadadhara,
Jayananda sings the Nadia-khanda in bliss.

Fragment 7. Nadia-khanda, section 18 (1971 ed., pp. 24–25)

The dress and beauty of the boy Gauranga; his mother fears the child-snatchers

[Narrative; disha. Raga Sindhura.]

1A silken dhoti, silken tassels,
beads of gold and silver;
necklaces of gems, pearls and coral,
a staff that enchants Madana.

2His body shines like the golden champaka,
flashing and glittering;
seeing his beauty, Madana-chand
dies and revives by turns.

3No longer does he go to play
on the town square:
the king's agent who snatches children
goes from house to house.40

4Abir, sandal, kunkuma, a topknot —
his holy body is fragrant;
in swarms the bees fly up
and roam about, greedy for honey.

5How many lightning-flashes
gleam upon your body!
Seeing your beauty, the wives of good families
cannot stay at home.

6A bakula garland on your curling locks,
your face an ocean of nectar;
with what deliberation
did the Creator fashion you!

7Jayananda says: "Listen, Shachi Thakurani:
let me die as a ransom for your son!"41

Fragment 8. Nadia-khanda, section 21 (1971 ed., pp. 27–28)

Gauranga picks up a puppy, names it Gangadasa and teaches it to repeat the name of Hari; the story of the cursed brahmana; the dog's liberation

[Narrative; disha.]

1Another day, within Navadvipa,
Gaura plays with the children from house to house.

2There were more boys than could be counted;
running up, he caught a puppy.

3Embracing it,42 the ocean of mercy says:
"At last fate has smiled on you!"

4He gave it the name Gangadasa,
put it on a chain and fed it rice with ghee.

5Where the child Gauranga was, there was Gangadasa;
he made the name of Hari sound forth from its mouth.

6"Say 'Hari', Gangadasa!" calls Gaurachandra;
hearing the sound "Hari", the dog cannot keep still.

7The Lord says: "This dog was a brahmana,
a great and zealous reviler of Vaishnavas.

8A Vaishnava begged food of him, and he would not give it:
'Shall a shudra, condemned by the Veda, eat rice in my house?'

9Mocking the Vaishnava, that brahmana bandied words with him;
in anger at this the Vaishnava cursed the brahmana.

10In his raving the brahmana gave the Vaishnava leftover food,
and by that curse he became a dog in Navadvipa."43

11When Gaurachandra had eaten, the remnants [were given to the dog],
and the dog's sin, the bond of its karma, came to an end.

12Eating the leftover rice, the dog Gangadasa
was rid of all its former offences.

13After some days the dog's curse came to an end:
giving up its life in the Ganga, the dog was liberated.

14Seeing the wonder, the people of Navadvipa were struck with awe:
by Gauranga's grace the dog Gangadasa was liberated.

15Boundless is Chaitanya's lila, delightful to hear:
the dog Gangadasa was freed from the bonds of existence.44

16Meditating on the two feet of Chaitanya and Gadadhara,
Jayananda sings the Nadia-khanda in bliss.

Fragment 9. Nadia-khanda, section 25 (1971 ed., pp. 32–33)

Gaurachandra's upanayana: the alms, the vow of silence, the brahmachari's food; the children's teasing; the blessing of his teachers Sudarshana and Gangadasa

[Then disha; narrative. "Glory, glory!"]

1The men and women who gave alms to Gaurachandra —
birth after birth Lakshmi will not leave their homes.45

2Nilambara Chakravarti completed the sacrifice with the final oblation,46
performed the anointing, applied the tilaka and offered the fees.

3Taking a vow of silence, Gaurachandra stayed at home;
his maternal grandmother fed him the plain havishya food.

4Vishvambhara slept on a fine throne;
Mishra Purandara taught him the morning sandhya.

5There were many heavenly women and brahmanas' wives;
the brahmanas bathed him with the five astringent decoctions and the five nectars.47

6"At midday eat the havishya food;
in the evening perform the sandhya and lie on a bed of kusha grass."

7Every day havishya food and the three sandhyas;
listening to kirtana, he forgot his childish games.

8[The children say:] "You've become a brahmachari, you eat havishya;
we are studying — why don't you go to study?

9Today you don't write in your copybook;
for three days you don't see a shudra's face."

10Hearing the children's words, Gaurachandra laughs;
with a sign he cleverly gave his mother to understand:

11"Give them all three moa balls each and milk laddus,
honour them all with garlands and sandal, and send them off."48

12So mother Shachi pacified them all;
then he told mother Shachi everything.

13For seven days he kept the vow of silence;
on the eighth day, with his guru's leave, he broke his silence.

14Sudarshana and Gangadasa, his two teachers,
came to bless him with a necklace of jewels.49

15He bowed down to his teacher and his teacher's wife;
seeing his divine form, everyone marvelled.

16Meditating on the two feet of Chaitanya and Gadadhara,
Jayananda sings the Nadia-khanda in bliss.

Fragment 10. Nadia-khanda, section 55 (1971 ed., pp. 64–65)

Lakshmi serves her mother-in-law; Gauranga hands the kitchen over to her; the feast for the Vaishnavas cooked by Lakshmi

[Narrative; disha.]

1Lakshmi Thakurani, serving Gaurachandra,
did not go to her father's house in the city of Nadia.

2She had nothing in her mind but serving her mother-in-law;
night and day she meditated on Gauranga's feet.

3One day Gauranga went to the kitchen
and, smiling and smiling, said to his mother:

4"Your aged body suffers so much;
let your daughter-in-law cook, and you eat.

5If you allow it, your daughter-in-law will serve you;
by serving you, Lakshmi will cross the ocean of existence.

6From today, mother, give up cooking;
eat what Lakshmi cooks."

7"Very well, very well," she agreed;
"from today the charge of the kitchen will be Lakshmi's."

8Hearing his mother's words, Gaurachandra laughs:
"Tomorrow I will feed Sri Haridasa.

9Srinivasa Pandita Thakura with his brothers, four in all,50
Vasudeva, Mukunda Datta, Jagai the scribe,

10Vakreshvara Pandita, Bhagai, Gangadasa —
tomorrow I will feed them with cakes and payasa.

11Invite all the Vaishnavas today:
tomorrow everyone eats Lakshmi's cooking."

12When night turned to dawn, Gaurachandra gave the order;
they called the maid Dukhi and Malini.51

13Some husk rice, some grate coconut,
some fill cakes with thickened milk.

14Some grind mung beans, some boil milk,
some grind turmeric and rice paste, some pound spices.

15Some bring firewood, some wash vegetables.52

16Lakshmi Thakurani bathed in the waters of the Ganga
and put on a wondrous, fine and lovely garment.

17Mother Lakshmi entered the kitchen;
Shachi Thakurani went there to watch.

18Merrily she cooked rice with fifty dishes,
cakes, payasa and rice, one after another.

19With sprigs of tulasi she offered it all to Krishna
and seated all the Vaishnavas in rows.

20She served everyone rice with ghee, shak, mung soup,
chhena curd, bari, laphra, patola, bathua;

21hing, hot dishes, jhol, fried things, tola, kanji-bara,
baramvu, sugar laddus, mitha-mukha, rolls of betel;

22khiri, amrita-gutika, khebara, nabat,
manohara, puri, dugdha-puli, sweets made of milk;

23coconut puli, shankar, kankara,
chandrakati, payasa, paramanna, sugar;

24gutika, dalima, honey, shravasat-puli,
mana-santosha, nayana-sukha, ganga-jala, shiyali;

25machchha-chhena, milk puli, koba, munda, cream —
an incomparable feast like Jagannatha's, the essence of all delight.53

26With cakes, drinks and food she gladdened the Vaishnavas
and adorned them all with garlands and sandal.

27She gave camphor betel, gave fine cloth;
giving a krishna-keli cloth, she pleased Srinivasa.

28To Sri Haridasa she gave a lakshmi-vilasa cloth;54
all the Vaishnavas went to their own homes.

29Thus Gaurachandra lives in Navadvipa;
Jayananda composes the song Chaitanya-mangala.

Fragment 11. Vairagya-khanda, section 24 (1971 ed., pp. 124–125)

Gauranga renounces worldly life; Nityananda arrives; Gauranga summons his companions to take sannyasa at Katwa

[Then the narrative; disha.]

1Agamas, nigamas, the Gita, a water-pot, a loincloth —
in renunciation he left the world and became detached.

2Leaving throne and bed, he sleeps on the ground;
he gave up the service of Vrinda and attendance on Krishna.

3Leaving his pleasures with Lakshmi, he lives under the trees;
in renunciation he gave up everything: soon he will take sannyasa.55

4Jewelled earrings, necklaces, golden amulets,
soft garments, the krishna-keli cloth — none of these he wears.

5The Lord gave up Vishnu oil and fragrant powder;
his curling locks are three parts grey with dust.

6The Thakura who wore divine garlands by the hundred —
that Lord now has on his neck a cord with knots for counting the Names.56

7The body that is grey with dust in the bliss of kirtana…57

8He in whose mouth was perfumed camphor betel —
that Lord eats haritaki: what joy is there in that?

9Seeing his great renunciation, his companions went mad with grief;
seeing this, Gauranga showed grace to them all.

10At this time Nityananda came to Navadvipa
and revealed to Gauranga all the secrets of sannyasa.

11Hearing this, Gaurachandra was filled with joy;
crossing the Ganga, Nityananda went on ahead.

12"Mukunda Datta the vaidya, Govinda the smith,58
come with me across the Ganga to Katwa.

13Acharyaratna Chandrashekhara, Acharya Hari,
Vasudeva Datta, Shuklambara Brahmachari,

14Vakreshvara Pandita, Bhagai, Gangadasa —
in your presence I will take sannyasa."

15Meditating on the two feet of Chaitanya and Gadadhara,
Jayananda composes the Vairagya-khanda in bliss.

Fragment 12. Utkala-khanda, section 16 (1971 ed., pp. 159–160)

At the Lion Gate Chaitanya proclaims the glory of the Vaishnavas: Krishna accepts their poor gifts, their food is his food, their dust purifies a whole family

[First, a disha on the glory of mahaprasada.]59

1One day Chaitanya Gosani, at the Lion Gate,
proclaimed to all the glory of the Vaishnavas:

2"Who can tell the birth and deeds of a Vaishnava?
Who can tell what caste a Vaishnava is?

3There is no distinction of caste for a Vaishnava in the world;60
Krishna always dwells in a Vaishnava's heart.

4With the Vaishnavas Krishna delights unceasingly;
by a Vaishnava's praise the Lord himself is won over.

5A Vaishnava's hut is Krishna's abode;
a Vaishnava's shak and rice are pure nectar.

6A handful of broken rice from a Vaishnava, water from his pot —
Krishna holds out his hand and takes it all.

7A Vaishnava's bed of grass, rice on a torn leaf —
in these Jagannatha finds joy as he eats and sleeps.

8A Vaishnava's necklace of gunja berries is equal to the Kaustubha gem;
[Krishna drinks] water from a Vaishnava's clay pot.

9A Vaishnava's seat of kasha grass, his haritaki fruit —
with these things of the Vaishnava Krishna is pleased.

10Over a Vaishnava the Holder of the Mountain holds a palm-leaf umbrella,
while at Indra's royal umbrella he does not even glance.

11A Vaishnava grinds nim wood and offers it to Krishna,
but scent and sandal from a non-Vaishnava he will not take.

12What a Vaishnava eats, Krishna eats;
where a Vaishnava goes, Krishna goes.

13When a Vaishnava is content, Krishna is content;
at the reviling of a Vaishnava Krishna is greatly angered.

14A Vaishnava's sorrow is Krishna's great sorrow;
from whomever a Vaishnava turns away, Krishna turns away.

15In whose house the dust of a Vaishnava's feet falls,
he goes, purified with all his family, to Vaikuntha.

16Wherever the water that has washed a Vaishnava's feet falls,
no misfortune ever befalls that place.

17A Vaishnava's eating is Krishna's eating;
a Vaishnava's rest is Krishna's rest.

18One should surely beg a Vaishnava's food and eat it;
and if one cannot get it, drink boiled water.61

19Not to eat it is to revile the Veda.
[Shloka:] "O Partha, […] the food of a Vaishnava […]"62

20Whosoever's body a Vaishnava's embrace touches,
the sins of his body go down to Rasatala.

21Whoever puts a garland and sandal on a Vaishnava's body,
whoever takes the leaf with the remains of a Vaishnava's meal,

22whoever walks round him and prostrates himself on the ground —
obtains in due order the fruit of all the tirthas, the Ganga first among them."63

23Meditating on the two feet of Chaitanya and Gadadhara,
Jayananda composes the Utkala-khanda in bliss.

Fragment 13. Prakasha-khanda, section 10 (1971 ed., pp. 193–196)

Chaitanya tells Ramananda Raya the tale of the raising of the banner: King Sumati and Queen Satyavati had been a sinful shudra and a fallen woman in a former birth, but were saved from hell because they set a rag on a pole over a deserted temple of Vishnu

[Then the narrative; disha.]

1In Nilachala, Chaitanya, sitting with his companions,
said with a smile to Raya Ramananda:

2"No lord like Krishna is seen in the three worlds:
whoever worships Krishna is delivered, by whatever way.

3In whatever manner a soul worships Krishna,
the worshipper of Krishna is honoured in the three worlds.

4The supreme Vaishnava, Gosani Narada Thakura —
at the mere hearing of his name sins depart.

5The great king Indradyumna asked him,
and Narada told the tale of the raising of the banner.

6Hear that tale, Ramananda Raya:
sinners and sinless alike are freed by Krishna's mercy.

7Long ago, in the Satya age, there was a universal king;
the king's name was Sumati, his wife's Satyavati.

8Born in the Lunar dynasty, the king was devoted to dharma;
sole sovereign over the seven islands.

9Pure and righteous, the king delighted in talk of Krishna;
calm, restrained, master of his senses, endowed with every virtue.

10King and queen both remembered their former births;
they were zealous in building temples, shrines, monasteries and waterworks.

11With divine service the king serves Krishna;64
the couple dance together throughout Jambudvipa.

12Satyavati, gathering many virtuous women,
dances in the temple, casting off shame.

13With a thousand disciples the sage Vibhandaka,
hearing of the king's renown, went to see him.

14On the day of Dvadashi the king was raising a banner;
just then Vibhandaka came to the royal gate.

15Offering water for the feet, arghya, water for sipping, sandal and garland,
the king seated the sage, worshipping him with the sixfold honours.

16"Today my night has turned to a happy dawn:
the sage Vibhandaka has come to my temple.

17Today I have reached my goal, my life has borne fruit:
I have had the sight of a greatly fortunate one."

18Vibhandaka says: "Come, universal king:
by the power of what merit did you become king of the seven islands?

19Why do all your women, casting off shame,
ceaselessly dance around the temple of Vishnu?65

20Tell me the reason for this, best of kings:
why are you so zealous in raising banners?"

21The king says: "I performed no dharma;
in my former birth I was a shudra named Malini.66

22My sins cannot be told;
I wandered through many lands with no one to help me.

23I stole the goods of the gods and the wealth of brahmanas;
wine, pork, consorting with harlots.

24I abandoned wife, son, mother, father and all my kin;
a great sinner, thief and robber, a very plague.

25For this reason, in grief of heart, I wandered without rest;
I ate the flesh of deer, killing deer without rest.

26In the hot season, tormented by hunger and thirst,
I suddenly saw a ruined temple there.

27Near it I saw a lake;
swans, karandava ducks and many birds fed there.

28On all four sides were flower gardens, the temple in the middle;
I drank the lake's water, cool as could be.

29I settled there, in the temple of Vishnu;
I roofed the broken house with grass, poles and laths.

30Plastering and sweeping the house, I lived there as a hunter,67
and for twenty years I lived by killing deer.

31At that time a wretched woman, a queen to be,68
leaving her family, came to me there.

32Dressed in worn clothes she came in the evening;
in her grief she came and met with me.

33Seeing this suffering woman, I was moved to pity;
seeing her anguish, I asked her everything:

34'What is your caste, where is your home, what is your name?' I asked.
'For what reason do you wander alone in the great forest?'

35I gave her cool water, meat and forest fruits;
when she had calmed herself, she told me everything:

36'I was born in a chandala family, Kuilini is my name;
proud of my beauty, I lived in the mountains.69

37My husband was handsome, steady, young and strong,
yet I gave myself to other men.

38Seeing my unfaithfulness, he cut off my nose and ears
and kept me bound on the bank of the Chausandi.70

39With other men a hundred times —
my husband would seize me and beat me without restraint.

40One day an evil thought came over me:
I put a chopper to his throat and killed my husband.

41Having killed such a husband, I went away;
I wander alone and find rest nowhere.'

42By the will of fate the two of us came together,
and for twenty-five years we kept house in that forest.

43In the rainy season, drunk with wine, dancing and dancing,
we suddenly tore a cloth and tied it to a pole.

44We planted that pole on the top of our hut;
in the wind the strip of cloth on the pole flew like a banner.

45At that moment a thunderbolt struck both our heads,
and both of us gave up our lives in that instant.

46Yama's messengers came and began to beat us;71
suddenly four messengers of Vishnu arrived there.

47Crying 'Let go, let go!' they struck with their maces;
the messengers of Vishnu came and rescued us both.

48Hear, Vibhandaka, how I went to Vaikuntha:
though I was a great sinner, I did not go to hell."

49Meditating on the two feet of Chaitanya and Gadadhara,
Jayananda sings the Prakasha-khanda in bliss.

Fragment 14. Vijaya-khanda, section 1 (1971 ed., pp. 215–216)

The beginning of the Vijaya-khanda; in Nilachala Chaitanya foretells to Gadadhara the evils of the Kali age: the decay of castes and rites, the rule of mlechchhas, the ruin of Varanasi, brahmanas in Persian dress, the impoverishment of the earth

[Then the narrative; disha.]

1Here the Tirtha-khanda came to its close;72
in the Vijaya-khanda Gauranga set out on his first journey.

2The Acharya Gosani with his companions is in Nilachala,
Nityananda Svarupa at the roots of the undying banyan.

3At this time Chaitanya, together with Gadadhara,
began, at his own pleasure, to speak of the future.

4All the wickedness that will be in the Kali age
he tells one by one, drawing out the essence:

5"The Veda will be taken from the brahmanas, Indra will withhold the rain;73
by various pretexts the king will seize all wealth.

6The earth will withhold her grain, kings will be of mlechchha race;
the kapila cow will withhold her milk, young women will be self-willed.

7The shudra will take the brahmana's Veda and the vaishya's calling;
brother will carry off sister — such will be the custom of the age.

8The sinful disciple will carry off his guru's wife;
all men of high caste will embezzle what is entrusted to them.

9The best men will steal the property of brahmanas and gods;
the low will become high, the best the basest.

10All trees and creepers will lose their nature;74
wives of good families will lose all shame and fear.

11The Ganga will withhold her waters, the tulasi will depart;
the yavanas will lay Varanasi waste.

12All the temples will lose their worship and service;
the tirthas will become inaccessible — know this for certain.

13The yavanas will break temples, shrines and monasteries;
brahmanas will abandon sandhya, the Veda and the worship of the gods.

14Kshatriyas will lose their valour, be jackals in battle;
the wealth of the other three castes will grow beyond measure.75

15Vaishyas will give up cattle-keeping, trade and the worship of the gods,
and all the shudras will give up serving the brahmanas.

16Avadhutas, ascetics and virtuous women will leave the earth;
all young widows will eat fish and meat.

17Son will defy father, disciple will defy guru;
brahmana widows will all eat flesh.

18Wife will defy husband, the world will be deceitful;
those born in good families will be wicked.

19Brahmanas will give up Ekadashi, sacrifice and charity;
shudras will expound the Puranas.

20Chandala and shudra women will keep Ekadashi;
the tulasi will leave the houses of the best people.

21Sannyasis will keep house with shudra women;
all who dwell at tirthas will hoard wealth.

22Brahmanas will keep house with shudra women;
everyone and anyone will keep house with brahmana women.

23Sannyasis will hoard wealth and trade;
Krishna will be served in shudras' temples.

24Brahmanas will sell lac, iron and salt;76
he who knows all the shastras will sell his daughter.

25Brahmanas will grow beards and speak Persian,77
wear socks and turbans and carry bows in their hands.

26The best of the twice-born will seek after mansabs,78
and constantly practise dacoity, theft and extortion at toll-posts.

27Shudras will worship images and shalagrama stones;
the sacred kapila cow will be sold for a copper coin.

28Ghee, honey, sesame, kusha grass, barley, sprouts,
curd, parched rice, durva grass, paddy, the svastika sign, vermilion —

29all these will leave the earth at the end of Kali;
no ashvattha, kadamba or nim will remain in the land.

30Conch, bell, mridanga, yak-tail whisk, canopy —
at the end of Kali all these will leave the earth.

31Cows will be like goats, clouds like dancers,79
men the size of a thumb, their speed like that of insects.

32Women will conceive at seven or eight years of age,
and from one womb five or seven children will be born.

33The shudra will be the world's guru, the mlechchha will be king;
the king will take everything, the subjects will be in misery.

34Sinners will live long, the virtuous will die early.80

35With little learning a man will be a great scholar,
with little wealth a great rich man.

36In the Kali age liberation is won by little merit;
'Blessed, thrice blessed is the Kali age!' all people sing."

37Meditating on the two feet of Chaitanya and Gadadhara,
Jayananda sings the Vijaya-khanda in bliss.

Fragment 15. Vijaya-khanda, section 5 (1971 ed., pp. 220–222)

At Shantipur: the young Achyutananda disputes with Advaita about Keshava Bharati; the leprous reviler of Vaishnavas; the festival on Madhavendra Puri's memorial day; at Kumarahatta the Lord tests Srinivasa; Raghava Pandita's shak at Panihati

1At Shantipur Chaitanya spends joyful time with Advaita;
in conversation Advaita is asked about a certain sannyasi:81

2"What is Keshava Bharati to Chaitanya?"
Advaita says: "He is his guru — listen, O wise one."

3Hearing this, Advaita's son Achyutananda
began a dispute with Acharya Gosani:

4"When you speak unworthily, Gosani, it pains me greatly:
Keshava Bharati the guru of Chaitanya Gosani?!"

5Achyutananda, a child of five,
like Kartikeya in beauty, was lovely to behold.

6He was a disciple of Gadadhara Pandita;
Advaita's son knows past and future.

7Ai Thakurani82 came to Advaita's house;
she showed great grace to Murari Gupta.

8At this time there came a leprous brahmana,
a reviler of Vaishnavas, devoted to the Veda.

9He had committed an offence at Srinivasa's door;
the Lord, showing him grace, gave him a command:

10"On the body of a reviler of Vaishnavas leprosy appears;
unseen and untouchable, he goes to Yama's abode.

11By the way a thorn goes in, by that way it comes out:
go and worship Srinivasa — he will help you."

12Acharya Gosani's guru, Madhavendra Puri,
once gave an instruction — I cannot fathom it.83

13The day of his memorial worship drew near;84
Ai Thakurani took charge of the cooking.

14Mukunda is the kirtana singer, Murari Gupta the storekeeper,
Bhavananda Adhikari sweeps and sprinkles water.

15Govinda and Govindananda blow the conches,
Buddhimanta Khan smears sandal on everyone.

16Chandrashekhara, Gopinatha, Srigarbha and Nandana —
these four brahmanas wave white chamaras.

17Damodara Svarupa and Paramananda Puri
direct the meal, canes in hand.

18How to serve patola, bathua and shak —
Vasudeva Datta knows this.

19Vakreshvara and Damodara hand out prasada garlands;
some eat prasada, some flattened rice and bananas.

20Ghee, honey, flattened rice, molasses, sugar candy, sugar;
in courtyards, on roads and at ghats, so many trays of flowers!85

21Mangoes, coconuts, jackfruit, curd, milk,
incense, lamps, sandal, aguru, barley, mung.

22"Eat, take, give!" — only this is heard;
Chaitanya, the crest-jewel, dances in bliss.

23At night people of every class come and go;
in the courtyards and roads of Shantipur everyone dances and sings.

24Night turned to dawn, the memorial worship was complete;
Thakura Gauranga set out for Kumarahatta.

25He stayed in Srinivasa's house at Kumarahatta;
Acharya Purandara questioned Vallabha Bhatta.86

26Shivananda Sena and Vasudeva Datta came there;
[the Lord] began to speak of Vasudeva's greatness:

27"I am Vasudeva's bought servant, listen, Srinivasa;87
Vasudeva Datta makes me manifest."

28He asked Srinivasa: "How do you manage?
Such a large household — what wealth do you spend on it?

29If your household cannot go on, listen, Srinivasa,
give up everything and take sannyasa."

30Clapping his hands three times, Srinivasa says:
"So be it, so be it! If it comes to three days' fasting,

31no, no, I will not go begging handfuls of rice from house to house88 —
I will tie a pitcher to my neck and drown myself in the Ganga."

32Hearing this, the ocean of mercy says with a smile:
"You will never know want again as long as you live."

33Then with hundreds of companions, together with Nityananda,
Gosani went joyfully to the village of Panihati.

34He ate in Raghava Pandita's house;
the Lord praised Raghava's shak and rice.

35"Gosani is very fond of shak and very fond of mangoes" —
Srinivasa says: "Raghava, long may you live, long may you live!"

36Nityananda says: "I have not eaten the shak:
Chaitanya Gosani is feeding it to everyone."

37A blessed abundance fell upon the shak:89 however much they spent,
however much shak they served, still more of it appeared.

38Even today it is proclaimed here in Panihati:
Raghava's shak and rice, so finely prepared.

39Meditating on the two feet of Chaitanya and Gadadhara,
Jayananda sings the Vijaya-khanda in bliss.

Notes

  1. The sections open with performance cues: "tataḥ kathā diśā", "kathā diśā" and the like. "Katha", "narrative", means recitation in payar; "disha" seems to indicate the refrain or the tune. Here and below such cues and raga names are given in square brackets in italics.
  2. The reading is doubtful: the transcription has "সুতার শঞ্চম(?) ঘড়", with a question mark. The translation is a conjecture.
  3. "Cottages with curved roofs": "বাঙ্গালি", probably buildings of the bangla type. "ধ্বজ কল হংস" is taken as "flags" and "kalahamsas"; the text may be corrupt.
  4. The end of the line ("লবঙ্গান্তশষ্পুরে") is corrupt; only "lavanga" (the clove tree) can be made out.
  5. "চন্দ্রার্ক তিলাকে", literally "with tilaka marks of moon and sun"; the sense is conjectural.
  6. "রক্ষ জাল মালা" is probably a corruption of "গবাক্ষ জাল মালা", "rows of latticed windows".
  7. Local names of rivers and waters around Jayapura; the Dhol-samudra and the Karati are unidentified.
  8. Literally "the great house of Ravi (the Sun)": perhaps the Solar dynasty, or an ancestor named Ravi.
  9. A single line: the second line of the couplet is missing from the text.
  10. Literally "Nanda and Yashoda took the water of the Yamuna"; understood as an oath taken with water in hand.
  11. That is, Nityananda's parents. Nityananda's father is usually called Hadai Pandita; the name "Paramananda" is unusual here.
  12. That is, Advaita's parents; other sources call them Kuvera Pandita and Labha (Nabha).
  13. The transcription has "ং্যান", an obvious misprint; read "ধ্যান", "meditation".
  14. "জন্মিল বৈদ্য বনিতা" may also be understood as "were born as vaidyas and as women".
  15. The stanza is defective: both its halves end with a double danda, and parts of lines seem to be lost or displaced. The "hour of cow-dust" (godhuli) is dusk.
  16. "শাখা": bangles of conch-shell, worn by married women; the word can also mean "branches".
  17. "রসবাটিকা", literally "little cup for juices (unguents)"; the exact sense is unclear. "ডাবর" is a basin or water vessel.
  18. "তিরোহিত" and "মুখারস মন্ডল" cannot be interpreted with confidence and are omitted; "সরঙ্গি" (a kind of platter) is kept as a name.
  19. "খড়িকা রঙ্গিকা পড়া": the sense is conjectural; "শাঁপুড়া", given as "little caskets", is also unclear.
  20. "গাঁঠ্যা কড়ি" is taken as "strung cowries", "কিআ পাতা" as ornaments shaped like ketaki leaves; "খুরে" in the last line is unclear.
  21. A list of fabrics and ornaments; many words ("তবক বসর পান কাটা", "শ্রীরাম খানি", "জমখা", "তারকা") are unclear and are rendered tentatively or omitted. "Lakshmi-vilasa" and "krishna-keli" (see Fragments 10 and 11) are names of costly fabrics.
  22. In the text couplets 6–7 form four lines on a single rhyme. Nityananda's initiation into sannyasa by Ishvara Puri is peculiar to Jayananda's version.
  23. The village "বামনবলা" in Vanga (East Bengal) is unidentified; Advaita's birthplace is usually given as Navagrama (Laur) in Srihatta.
  24. Piralya (পিরল্যা): a village of yavanas (Muslims) near Navadvipa.
  25. "গন্ধর্বে লিখন আছে ধনুর্ময় প্রজা": the sense is unclear; "ধনুর্ময়", "armed with the bow", is used below (couplet 29) as an epithet of Prataparudra ("warlike").
  26. The couplet lists scholars of Navadvipa; the names Vidya-virinchi and Vidyaranya are unidentified, and the sense of the second line is conjectural.
  27. "নাকে খত দিল", literally "gave a bond with his nose", i.e. humbly owned his fault, rubbing his nose on the ground.
  28. Literally "shall be fined with the royal tax and mount the trident"; the "trident" (ত্রিশূল) is the stake for execution.
  29. "আপন ইৎসাএ মার প্রাণে পাছে রাখ": the sense is unclear; it may also mean "beat him at your will, but leave him alive".
  30. The second line is shorter than the norm; part of it seems to be lost.
  31. "কলেতে" is taken as "কোলেতে", "in the lap, in the arms".
  32. "কত না খায় তুমি মাএর মাথা", literally "how much of your mother's head you eat": an affectionate mother's oath ("to eat someone's head" is to be their ruin); the sense is given approximately.
  33. The refrain of the lullaby; "o nā āy āy" is a crooning sound for lulling a child.
  34. "দে" is taken as "দেও", "demon": the evil eye or a spell is meant.
  35. Literally "a wish arose in Shachi Thakurani's heart"; the sense is unclear.
  36. "কয়া খেড়ি": some children's game (perhaps with shells or pebbles); the name is unidentified.
  37. A ghati is a measure of time of about 24 minutes.
  38. "হাপুতি": a mother whose children have died (cf. Shachi's eight daughters in Fragment 4). "বাপের ঠাকুর" and "গোশারি" (probably "গোসাঞি", "lord") are terms of endearment; the translation is approximate.
  39. "ততদিন সংসার আচারভ্রষ্ট নহে", literally "so long [one] in the world does not fall from the rules"; understood as advice to keep custom until realization is reached.
  40. "ছাল্যা ধরা রাজার দূত", literally "the king's messenger who seizes children"; apparently a bogey with which the mother keeps her son at home. The stanza is spoken by Shachi.
  41. "নিছনি": a rite in which something is waved around a loved one and given away in their stead to avert misfortune; the poet offers himself in Gauranga's place.
  42. The transcription has "তীরে" ("on the bank"); by the sense we read "তারে", "it".
  43. Couplets 9–10 are obscure in places ("ভান্ডি", "প্রলাপে"); apparently the brahmana was punished for insulting the Vaishnava and giving him leftovers.
  44. The transcription has "ভবনন্দ", probably a misprint for "ভববন্ধ", "the bonds of existence".
  45. After investiture with the sacred thread the new brahmachari goes round begging alms. "গারি" is taken as "home"; the reading is uncertain.
  46. Nilambara Chakravarti is Gaurachandra's maternal grandfather. "জংগ্যে পূর্ণা দিল" is taken as "পূর্ণাহুতি", the concluding oblation into the fire.
  47. The five astringent decoctions (pancha-kashaya) are made from the bark of sacred trees; the five nectars (panchamrita) are milk, curd, ghee, honey and sugar.
  48. Moa: sweet balls of puffed rice and molasses; laddus: sweet balls.
  49. "রত্নমালা ছিরু": the second word is unclear; the translation is conjectural.
  50. Jayananda's Srinivasa Pandita is Srivasa Pandita, the eldest of four brothers (Srivasa, Srirama, Sripati, Srinidhi). The line may also be read "Srinivasa Pandita Thakura and [his] four brothers".
  51. Dukhi was a maidservant in Srivasa's house; Malini was Srivasa's wife.
  52. A single line: the second line of the couplet is missing from the text.
  53. Couplets 20–25 are a list of dishes and sweets; many names (laphra, tola, baramvu, khebara, shankar, kankara, chandrakati, dalima, shravasat-puli, shiyali, machchha-chhena, koba, munda, etc.) cannot be identified precisely and are transliterated. "Mana-santosha" ("delight of the mind"), "nayana-sukha" ("joy of the eyes") and "ganga-jala" ("Ganga water") are names of sweets. Shak is stewed greens, bari are dried balls of pulse paste, bathua (বাস্তুক) is goosefoot, jhol is a thin curry, kanji is sour rice-water, nabat is sugar candy, puli and puri are kinds of cakes, payasa and paramanna are rice cooked in milk.
  54. "Krishna-keli" and "lakshmi-vilasa" are names of costly fabrics (cf. Fragment 3).
